extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers of journalism and mass communication; journalism practitioners interested in sources and external influences on news content
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and factors that influence which sources, events, and topics appear in news coverage and how media content is shaped by outside organizations (interest groups, PR, advertisers, other media). Focuses on source availability, type of event, institutional incentives, and market pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists will cover individual sources when they are available; organizations often go out of their way to be available, whereas individuals rarely have sufficient time or resources to compete effectively for the journalists' attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Of all sources the journalists had contact with, 96 percent of individual sources were covered, compared with only 71 percent of organizational sources; the issue is availability and resources to be accessible to journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of event affects source type
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature of the news event may affect whether individual or organizational sources are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories about the plight of people—such as a kidnapping—have strong human interest and therefore individual sources may seem more appropriate; because such events often are played out over several days, journalists also have more time than usual to locate and interview individuals (Atwater & Green, 1988).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for official sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Official sources (government officials, police) are often preferred by journalists because they are more easily available and are believed to have important things to say.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists and editors tend to accept the things official sources say as factual; interviewing an official source makes the journalists' job efficient by concentrating on individuals with important things to say and by eliminating the need to double- and triple-check 'facts' (Paletz & Entman, 1981; Hackett, 1985).

rubrics_metrics.name: Displacement of technical expertise by officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters may rely more on government sources than on technical experts who could provide scientific background or safety-minimizing information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In coverage of environmental disasters reporters were more likely to rely on government sources than on technical experts (Hornig, Walters, & Templin, 1991).

rubrics_metrics.name: Media-type and outlet differences in source reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Different news outlets and media types rely on different source mixes (e.g., print vs TV, wire services vs local reporters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Print media sources (Newsweek, NYT, WSJ) relied more on Wall Street sources for the 1987 stock market crash, whereas CBS News relied more on government officials (Lasorsa & Reese, 1990); wire service reporters under stringent time constraints are most likely to rely on official activities and on the governor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time constraints and reporter routine
rubrics_metrics.description: Time pressure and reporting routine affect the range and type of sources used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wire service reporters, under the most stringent time constraints, are most likely to rely on official activities; reliance on a narrow range of sources may be a function of institutional factors such as part-time legislatures (Fico, 1984a, 1984b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Location/proximity of news organization
rubrics_metrics.description: The distance of a news organization from the event influences reliance on official versus nonofficial sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations farthest from the city in which an event occurs will rely primarily on official sources (Martin, 1988).

rubrics_metrics.name: Story type: issues vs events
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a story is about an ongoing issue (e.g., legislation) or a discrete event affects source selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In stories about issues, official sources may be most common because of their vested interest in the debate's outcome; when the story is about an event, especially human interest, unofficial sources may get more play (example: officials accounted for only 30 percent of network sound bites about the 1985 TWA hijacking).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of confidential/unnamed sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Some official sources provide information but do not want to be personally identified and are used for background or to test ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confidential sources may provide information to let the public know something, provide background information, or test the viability of an idea with a 'trial balloon'; many derive satisfaction or benefit from giving information (Gassaway, 1988).

rubrics_metrics.name: Source personality and interpersonal attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: A source's personality—extroversion, assertiveness, perceived credibility, accessibility, and quotability—affects their prominence and dominance in news coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extroverted U.S. presidents got two to three times the front-page coverage of introverted peers (Streitmatter, 1985); assertiveness, credibility (as determined by the journalist), accessibility, and quotability affect both frequency of mention (prominence) and tendency to be quoted rather than reported about (dominance) (Stempel & Culbertson, 1984).

rubrics_metrics.name: Powerful actors' agenda-setting and media management
rubrics_metrics.description: Powerful individuals and institutions (e.g., the U.S. president) can create and orchestrate news to set the terms of public-political discourse and influence media coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The president has a natural advantage because he is invariably news; administrations can 'work the system' to create news necessary to give the president's agenda wide publicity and dominance (Bernard Cohen / Gannett Center quote). Example: Ronald Reagan orchestrated encounters and 'passing from the White House to the helicopter' to emphasize items he wanted covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest groups providing coverage guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest groups sometimes seek to influence media content by providing 'guidelines' for covering topics of interest (e.g., ABA 'fair trial-free press' guidelines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By 1976 many states had adopted voluntary press-bar guidelines specifying how media should cover crime and trials, but newspapers operating under voluntary agreements were no more likely to follow guidelines than those without agreements (Tankard, Middleton, & Rimmer, 1979).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest-group lobbying and media criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest groups lobby other groups and criticize media to change media content and practices, sometimes using media attention to press for revisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interest groups may lobby another group to persuade the mass media on the first group's behalf and may criticize the media so the criticisms get on the news agenda and cause revisions of media practices or policies (example: Austin Society to Oppose Pseudoscience).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest groups' direct pressure on advertisers (boycotts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest groups use organized pressure on advertisers (boycotts, form letters) to influence programming and content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: American Family Association urged supporters to mail protest postcards to sponsors and to boycott advertisers of offending programs; example where contacting General Mills led to cancellation of advertising spending on 'SNL'—demonstrating that advertiser pressure can change sponsorship decisions and thereby content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest groups as agenda-setters via media-created events
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest groups design and hold events (demonstrations, protests) that are more likely to be covered than real events; these 'pseudoevents' serve both the group's need for coverage and the media's need for news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boorstin's pseudoevent characteristics: not spontaneous, planted to be reported, relation to reality ambiguous, often self-fulfilling; interest groups play to media's demand for 'new' news by providing such events, which are more likely to be covered than real events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations (PR) influence through press materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations campaigns influence media coverage directly (press releases) and indirectly (calling attention to issues); PR materials often generate substantial newsroom use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence shows many news stories begin from press releases, indicating the importance of PR materials for the contemporary press (Turow, 1989); PR messages may have cognitive goals (informing/warning) as well as persuasive goals (Shoemaker, 1989).

rubrics_metrics.name: PR industry trends affecting influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural trends in the PR industry (consolidation, internationalization, reliance on market research) affect how PR shapes media content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three trends: increasing consolidation of ownership among largest firms (PR conglomerates), increasing international operations, and growing importance of market research sometimes overshadowing traditional personal contact (Dilenschneider, 1990).

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists' and PR practitioners' similar news judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists and PR practitioners often have remarkably similar judgments about what is newsworthy, influencing how PR materials are received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists may perceive a larger gap than actually exists; many PR practitioners were once journalists and share news values, which may increase PR efficacy (Kopenhaver, Martinson, & Ryan, 1984).

rubrics_metrics.name: Other media organizations as influential sources/agenda-setters
rubrics_metrics.description: Media organizations themselves act as sources for other media and can set the agenda across outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: New England Journal of Medicine often quoted for medical news because it reflects conflict within medicine; the New York Times is treated as the final arbiter of quality and professionalism and often 'takes the lead' in coverage; NPR is seen as a positive influence by many journalists; wire services transmit stories that are picked up widely (with qualifications about causality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wire services' role in story transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Wire services transmit stories from town to town and may act as powerful agenda-setters for daily newspapers, though causation is contested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some studies show newspapers publish similar content in proportions to what wire services transmit, but other explanations (shared notions of newsworthiness) may account for similarities (Whitney & Becker, 1982; Todd, 1983).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising as primary revenue influence on content
rubrics_metrics.description: Because advertisers buy the audience, advertising interests directly and indirectly shape media content; human attention becomes a commodity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertising pays a substantial portion of media costs; owners orient content toward the interests of those who finance the press (Altschull, 1984); 'one percentage point for a network in prime-time audience share represents more than $30 million' (Bagdikian, 1989).

rubrics_metrics.name: Target audience definition influences content
rubrics_metrics.description: Media tailor content to attract and retain the target audience defined by demographics (age, gender, income, education) and psychographics (attitudes, lifestyles), because advertisers buy access to those segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers focus circulation and content toward upscale target audiences attractive to advertisers (e.g., Wall Street Journal, Boston Globe—high-income readers); magazines/newspapers publish different fiction/news based on target audience (Cantor & Jones, 1983).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising economics and circulation strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising rate calculations (cost per thousand) and the economics of circulation influence editorial and distribution strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having more subscribers increases advertising income up to a point; beyond that advertisers may not pay proportionally more, leading magazines to change frequency or distribution; subscription charges can function to 'qualify' readers for advertisers (Peterson, 1981; Rosse, 1981).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience/market pressures on newsroom decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsrooms and journalists, socialized to advertiser-funded media, are attentive to audience tastes and ratings, which can influence story selection and presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low newscast ratings may be blamed on news staff and lead them to produce content the audience will watch; journalists' routines are shaped by the need to capture the 'right' target audience for advertisers (Altheide, 1976).
